美国10.8万亿美元401(k)即将打开加密投资通道，几个核心问题：

Q1：提交白宫OIRA最终审查后，还要多久？

通常审查周期为90天，也可以提前结束或延期。按照11月5日提交计算，预计2027年1—2月有望完成审查。

Q2：什么时候真正可以买比特币？

预计2027年上半年有机会正式发布并逐步生效，2027年下半年至2028年可能看到更多401(k)计划开放加密投资。

但规则生效不等于所有退休账户自动可以买币，最终由雇主和计划受托人决定。

Q3：民主党控制参众两院，能阻止吗？

可以反对，可以监督，也可以尝试通过《国会审查法》（CRA）推翻规则。

但需要两院通过决议并由总统签署。如果特朗普否决，还需要两院分别获得三分之二多数才能推翻否决。

Q4：特朗普有权推动吗？

有。特朗普已经签署行政令14330，要求劳工部推动401(k)另类资产投资规则改革。

具体规则由劳工部制定，白宫OIRA负责最终审查，不需要国会重新通过一部法律。

Q5：最终可能有多少资金进入加密市场？

美国401(k)资产规模约10.8万亿美元。

按照未来3—5年的采用情况，我的情景估算：

保守：约5亿—25亿美元

text:
New Emerging Managers episode with Paavan Gami (@hiro_sugimoto_) of Raas Partners is live, our first with a public equities fund manager

Before starting Raas, Paavan spent 5 years at Greenoaks, where he was part of the now legendary Carvana trade (if you read Colossus’ Neil Mehta profile, you know the one). They sold before the crash in ‘21, bought back in after a 90% drop, then kept buying through another 75% drawdown while LPs told Neil the company was going bankrupt. They ended up owning ~4% of Carvana, a stake worth $1B+ by 2025, and the stock went on to 100x off its 2022 low

His line on how you get comfortable doing that stuck with me: “it’s very hard to run into a burning building if you don’t know the structure of that building already.”

Then he left one of the best seats in investing to make a 20-year bet on India. Beyond the macro case everyone knows (1.5B people, half under 30, 6%+ real growth a year for 25 years), his bigger thesis is that stock picking in India has far more alpha than in the US, for structural reasons:

- Private capital is thin, so the best companies go public early. That means you can basically do Series B/C-style growth investing in public markets
- The index is mostly state-owned companies, metals, mining, oil and gas (only 1 internet company in the top 50), so the market still doesn’t know how to price tech
- Most consumer categories are still ~90% mom-and-pops, so the leader at 5% share can compound to 30-40%

We get into all of it, plus whether AI breaks the India story (I’m more worried than he is), the two businesses he’s “married” (Eternal and Meesho), and how he uses AI agents in his process

(Disclosure: I’m an LP in Raas Partners)

“What makes the value of a company is its product and revenue. What makes the value of a token is its community. And I think the Bitcoin community became really toxic and did not really wanna evolve over time.”

author: brezshares
quoted_text:
Ansem shares his long-term thesis on Pearl ($PEARL), dubbed as "AI Bitcoin," and why it could hit escape velocity

“Pearl high risk for sure, but what they're trying to do is be a form of hard money in the same way that Zcash ($ZEC) is trying to be a form of hard money.”

 “But their entire thesis is that instead of just doing proof of work where the work that you're doing isn't worth anything, it's just electricity cost, compute cost.”

"The compute that you use to mine Pearl can also be used for all the AI inference matrix multiplications that you need whenever you're doing inference.”

 “They call it 'useful work' when you're mining Pearl, where you can also make money by serving that inference to people.”

“And that does make sense as a thesis if you think how much compute we're going to be using over time is going to continue to go up.”

“Pearl could hit escape velocity as being a hard form of money, 'AI Bitcoin' is what they call it.”

text:
People will talk about “storytelling” and then it’s just a bucket of loosely connected facts

Storytelling requires a story

A story has a beginning, middle, end. A protagonist, an antagonist. Maybe a loyal sidekick. A noble quest. A surprise! A pickle!! A change, a resolution.

It’s the difference between “in a galaxy far far away…” and “today we’re excited to announce that we are launching a rebel alliance”

In some stories, the protagonist is you, on your own hero’s journey

Other times, the protagonist is the customer. They have an important goal, but there’s something standing in the way. What has changed now, and why? What’s their happy ending?

text:
hearing some chatter that anthropic is now lowering down to $1tn to get this IPO done. let me explain why this doesnt matter and its actually all over-

the entire existence of this company is based on a funding model that inherently has extreme asset liability mismatch. what that means is that just like the hyperscalers are diluting their equity fund capex, there is an expectation that anthropic will also have to do the same. ie it needs strong equity to perpetuate the scheme

but if you IPO at the wrong price (and dont get a pop which increasingly appears they wont be; spacex already below) then youre now in the death spiral that crypto investors should be very familiar with: its called the reflexivity trap of the confidence game. its the "ill bid FTT at $22 all day" or the "steady lads UST is $1" game, with all its lucid horrors. and here is the key insight- the confidence game exists at the service of the creditors. if there is no credit, there is simply no equity. and there is no credit, if there is no collateral

if the credit rating agencies are not going to give IG at $2tn, they are certaintly not going a better HY rating at $1tn. and there is no world in which anthropic can exist without credit because ~$1tn of commit, much of which is noncancellable, is a straight up negative equity pledge

yet there were two scenarios in which i was willing to concede anthropic could IPO: first 1) the improbable but possible was if the hyperscalers/chips oligopoly came to rescue and plug the hole, given their incestuous nature of revenue bookings and paper gains/losses at scale. but it is clear now that the market has spoken this will lead to a mutual death, and should not be attempted. or perversely even better, they are actually better off letting anthropic go to zero so they can acquire the pieces on the cheap which is the best nash equilibrium outcome, not just for the dominant player but for society at large. second 2) the us government can nationalize the company and collude with other sovereigns (like UAE, Saudi, Japan who are basically already the checks) to force its funding as a collective bargain. this gives you trillions, which is actually the most effective backstop to restore market confidence. the first edge case does require an IPO, but the second edge case here for which i believe there is still a good chance that this is the ultimate end game- will require a failed IPO to recapitalize at a normalized price for the consortium (and dont forget that openai front ran this investor group in anticipation of this dynamic to play out as a private co last month)

i believe the market is crapping out today because the market is recognizing it will not IPO. and actually, as ive said before, this is a very good thing. i might even imagine that the market could quickly rebound on the news of its IPO being delayed because it allows #2) to play out, as not only a national, but an international bailout. the US is more likely to tolerate, even relish, the taxes of foreginers to fund our domestic companies. that is the only end game that really matters, and the end game i am going to be excited to see

we'll see if this newly revamped washington can figure it out

这里再给大家说一下这个项目的机制吧，它相当于是 NFT 的一个庞氏螺旋

首先，你在平台上购买一个 Machine，就会获得对应的 ERC404 图币转换NFT

这个 NFT 有两种玩法：

不质押： 保留代币的流动性，赌币价上涨，涨了直接卖出。

选择质押吃税： 一旦质押，就无法再换回代币，这个过程不可逆。

不过质押后的 NFT 可以在二级市场交易，类似 OpenSea，只是目前二级市场还没开放。

整个逻辑其实就是一个正反馈循环：

代币交易量增加 → 交易税收入增加 → NFT 质押收益提高 → 吸引更多人质押 → 代币流通量减少 → 币价上涨 → NFT 估值上涨 → 吸引更多资金和交易量进入。

然后继续循环。

说白了，就是利用交易税作为收益来源，再通过不可逆质押减少代币流通量，试图同时推动币价和 NFT 价格上涨。

这样一个庞氏螺旋项目，目前市值居然还不到 200K，我觉得确实挺离谱的

quoted_text:
$ZEC is an extremely misunderstood asset, which is why there's still so much upside left.

ZEC started to bottom around April 2025, when @ebfull shared a blog post about Project Tachyon. Tachyon makes Zcash quantum proof and paves the way to scale Zcash to 50k TPS. And you cannot address quantum without addressing scalability since post-quantum cryptographic signatures are going to be an order of magnitude larger.

At the risk of sounding hyperbolic, the real bull case for Zcash is to fulfill Satoshi's vision: becoming peer-to-peer electronic digital cash. What many Bitcoiners gave up on. Zcash has the same properties as BTC, except it has a credible roadmap to scale to 50k TPS at the base layer, with built-in privacy. It's extremely ambitious, but that is the vision.

At the same time, I expect Bitcoin to undergo a crisis of confidence. Crypto participants have been conditioned to blindly believe BTC will hit new highs every couple of years. I believe these assumptions will be challenged as the quantum overhang looms large, and continued underperformance will drive more flows into ZEC. I would not be surprised if BTC trades like ETH last cycle.

Peter Thiel talks about the "Last Mover Advantage." That is, it's far better to make the last great development in a market and then dominate. Facebook vs Myspace. Google vs Yahoo. Zcash has dominated a small niche (privacy), and then it plans to scale to the ambitious goal, which is peer-to-peer electronic cash.

The ZEC trade closely resembles the SOL trade last cycle. ZEC's ability to move fast challenges a slow-moving incumbent (BTC), similar to how SOL challenged the ivory tower of ETH. History doesn't repeat, but it often rhymes.

There’s a fundamental mismatch between why Zcash is going up (Tachyon + last mover advantage) and the broader market’s understanding ("just a privacy coin"). Understanding this is a form of alpha/edge. I expect this knowledge gap to close when Tachyon hits mainnet in Q1 2027.

As a result, I expect the following over the next 1-2yrs:
1) Bitcoiners will start "silent quitting" and begin hedging their holdings with ZEC
2) Capital allocators that may have full ported BTC 5 years ago, will buy both ZEC and BTC as a bet on a sovereign SoV
3) Smart crypto developers to move on from other ecosystems to start contributing to Zcash
4) As ZEC continues to outperform BTC, people will start to seriously entertain the possibility of a flippening
5) $20,000 ZEC

Zigher.

text:
i’m building Concrete, a systems programming language designed around formal verification and observability

programming languages were historically designed for humans to express ideas and write code efficiently. but if AI is going to write most of the code, the optimization problem changes

we can afford to use smaller, more restrictive languages if that makes programs easier to reason about and formally verify

memory safety is only one property we care about. what about proving that a function cannot access the network, doesn’t allocate, preserves an invariant, or satisfies a mathematical specification?

i am building a language where the compiler can produce machine-checkable evidence about what a program does in every level before the code even runs

Concrete is built around that idea. it has linear types for explicit resource management, no garbage collector, no implicit destruction, restricted borrowing, and a small core formalized in Lean

it also has an explicit capability system: functions must declare what they’re allowed to do, such as accessing files, allocating memory, or performing I/O. this lets the compiler reason about side effects across the entire program

we deliberately restrict features like closures, dynamic dispatch, and hidden control flow to make whole-program analysis and formal verification more tractable

the first version of concrete is implemented in lean4 and you can write the proofs in lean4 too. in the future we will support other formal verification languages too.

let’s see how it goes. wish me luck and give it a star

币安办学习营，其实就是希望能和社区有更多面对面交流的机会。

最初的想法也非常简单。一方面，面对面交流，能听到很多平时在线上可能不太好表达的观点和信息。另一方面，我们也确实希望通过这样的交流，让社区能更完整地了解我们。

我相信，对于用户和从业者来说，无论是关注还是来参加这样的活动，大多都是带着善意的。

但就是这样一个活动，这两天还是出现了一些明显不符合事实的讨论。对于这些声音，我们不想去揣测动机，但确实让人感受到了一些恶意。这对于所有参加活动的朋友，特别是对那些认真交流的人来说，其实是很不公平的。

当然，我们也相信活动本身肯定也有不够完善的地方，对于理性的批评和建议，我们一直愿意听，也希望能够不断改进。

其实说到底，币安也是一家商业机构，同样要遵循市场的规律。我始终相信，一家企业能够长期走下去，归根结底还是因为它能够持续为用户和行业创造价值。

币安能够发展到今天的规模，离不开过去为用户创造的实际价值，也离不开大家长期以来的信任和选择。规模本身没什么值得炫耀的，它更多是价值创造之后的结果。如果有一天，我们不能继续为用户创造价值，那么今天的规模也就失去了意义。

我想表达的是，我们希望我们能够始终带着善意做事，坚持对用户有益的方向，把更多精力放在真正有价值的事情上。而不是其他。

相信时间会检验很多事情，行动也比言语更有说服力。

月底 BBW，期待曼谷再见！💛

Ansem shares his long-term thesis on Pearl ($PEARL), dubbed as "AI Bitcoin," and why it could hit escape velocity

“Pearl high risk for sure, but what they're trying to do is be a form of hard money in the same way that Zcash ($ZEC) is trying to be a form of hard money.”

 “But their entire thesis is that instead of just doing proof of work where the work that you're doing isn't worth anything, it's just electricity cost, compute cost.”

"The compute that you use to mine Pearl can also be used for all the AI inference matrix multiplications that you need whenever you're doing inference.”

 “They call it 'useful work' when you're mining Pearl, where you can also make money by serving that inference to people.”

“And that does make sense as a thesis if you think how much compute we're going to be using over time is going to continue to go up.”

“Pearl could hit escape velocity as being a hard form of money, 'AI Bitcoin' is what they call it.”

We’re launching VIALS-AA, a leaderboard for Handshake AI’s VIALS benchmark for visual reasoning in life sciences and biotech research

Visual artifacts are central to how scientists analyze experiments and make research decisions, but interpreting them correctly remains a challenge for frontier models. VIALS’ 161 tasks span eight domains and need models to reason over artifacts including gel blots, flow cytometry plots, plasmid maps, and phylogenies. Each task requires models to interpret an artifact and draw a specific scientific conclusion.

We evaluate models by running each task three times in Stirrup, our open source agent harness, with code execution and image inspection tools. GPT-6 Luna (medium) grades each answer against the reference answer, and we report the share of tasks judged correct in all three repeats (pass^3).

Key takeaways:

➤ The top three models are separated by 3 points: Gemini 4 Carbon (high) from @GoogleDeepMind leads narrowly with 64%, followed by GPT-6 Astra (max) from @OpenAI at 63% and Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) from @AnthropicAI at 61%

➤ Astra and Sol achieve similar scores to Opus and Sonnet at a much lower Cost per Task: Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) averages $1.64 per task, ~29× as much as Sol (~$0.056). This price difference is significantly driven by turn use - GPT-6 Astra (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) average ~8 turns per task, compared with ~27 for Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) and ~25 for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback)

➤ Open weights models trail the highest score by ~19 points: Kimi K3.1 Pro leads open weights models on VIALS-AA at 45%, narrowly ahead of MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 43%

➤ 14 of 161 tasks saw safety refusals on at least one model: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) refused on 6 tasks, the most of any model, and half of the 14 affected tasks saw refusals from multiple models

Thank you to @joinHandshakeAI and the VIALS authors for creating the benchmark and collaborating with us on bringing it to Artificial Analysis!

quoted_text:
Today, Injective made history by ringing the opening bell at Nasdaq to celebrate the launch of the $INJ Staked ETF, becoming one of the only crypto assets to have an official U.S. listed ETF.

A few years ago Injective was just an idea.

I remember my first day in the middle of COVID in 2020 sharing one desk in a coworking space with @ericinjective because that’s all we could afford. We took effectively zero salary while working 18 hour shifts. No one around me understood exactly why I would dive headfirst into such uncharted waters in an industry that seemed doomed to fail according to all the tech and mainstream pundits.

Our goal of creating a blockchain just for finance was so outlandish that fundraising became a literal nightmare. It couldn't be done, too complex, too many variables and not enough upside in an already crowded field of crypto competitors according to the VCs.

But through all the struggle and pain, I knew with the family I found here at Injective I could achieve anything. Despite the bad press that seemed to surround crypto, draconian regulations designed to impede our progress, massive hacks in the industry and the downfall of once lauded companies, Injective survived it all.

And over time we found others who started to believe in our vision. Slowly but surely, we built a massive coalition of users, traders, builders, institutions and everyday people who believed in bringing financial freedom to all through the tech we were building. We brought major funds to our corner from Binance all the way to legendary entrepreneurs like Mark Cuban. And what was once just an idea being built by a few crazy kids in the middle of COVID became not just a unicorn but an absolute force in the blockchain industry that would redefine what the internet economy can look like in the 21st century.

Today, we have built a team of 70 of the smartest and hardest working people I have ever come across. We have reached millions of new users and community members. We have brought some of the world's largest banks, enterprises and financial institutions onchain with global giants like Google Cloud and LG joining our ecosystem. We have brought billions of dollars in tokenized real world assets to our chain. We also overcame years of regulatory hurdles and today have become the first layer 1 blockchain ecosystem with an SEC registered transfer agent, enabling us to lead the new era of tokenized markets.

And we're now working at the absolute frontier of the next era of finance. From tokenization and real world assets to institutional grade infrastructure and the emerging onchain agentic economy, we're building the foundations for an entirely new financial system.

More than anything else, Injective has taught me that the only limit to what you can achieve in this life is your own inner drive. And anything worth achieving was never meant to be easy.

I will forever be grateful for this opportunity to play a role in this journey. My team and I will not rest until we have truly created a new financial system that democratizes real financial opportunity for all.

Our best days are still ahead of us. We have an entire financial system to change and we're only getting started 🥷

quoted_text:
This report on AI R&D automation (RSI) is a big update towards ASI within 1-2 years. It says AI progress is sped up by RSI right now by around 2x. In AI 2027, this happens around March 2027.

I was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026 (around 1.15x-1.3x). It seems as though there was specific privately available evidence that would have changed my mind.

I haven't seen an unredacted version of this report; this is purely about the public report. Because so much of the underlying evidence was redacted from the public report, I think conclusions about things other than the observed 2x faster rate of progress on benchmarks depend significantly on trust for the authors of the report. (E.g., conclusions about whether this speed up is from RSI depend on trust.) I do trust the authors of the report a lot to be careful and rigorous and generally do a good job. (Note that I also work at METR.) Less extensive redactions would greatly reduce this need for trust.

Since in my current role I may have access to other confidential information that could be relevant to timelines one way or another, I unfortunately cannot state my all-things-considered views on ASI timelines or the probability of a software intelligence explosion right now. Here, I’ve done some analysis of the implications using my previous public statements.

A 2x acceleration in overall AI progress from RSI corresponds to a much larger than 2x RSI speed up for AI software R&D (algorithms and data); I did an estimate using my public preexisting modeling of drivers of AI progress and the public report which yielded a very rough estimate of 4.5x for how much RSI is currently accelerating AI software progress (relative to no AI automation). In the AI 2027 scenario, this much acceleration happens around March 2027.

Here are the worked details of this estimate based on my public modeling. There are two main reasons RSI speed up of AI software R&D must be larger:

- Not all of AI progress is from better software (some is from scaling up compute in training runs). I've previously speculated that around 2/3 of AI progress is from software improvements which implies that 2x overall AI progress acceleration requires 3x faster software progress.
- Diminishing returns: A fixed amount of progress requires more work over time, so to ongoingly maintain 3x faster software progress via AI automation, you need increasingly large speed boosts from AI automation (as in, speed ups relative to how fast software R&D would go without AI automation). Based on this report, it seems that there is a substantial amount of additional AI progress from automation that has occurred.

We can estimate the effects of diminishing returns by first determining how many additional years of software progress we've seen (relative to the preexisting trend) and then estimating how much software R&D would slow down after a year of software progress if you held inputs fixed due to diminishing returns. I've previously estimated software R&D would slow down by around 2x for each year of software progress if you held inputs fixed (https://t.co/AYhl9hyiAj) and based on the report, it seems as though we've perhaps seen roughly 0.35-1.0 years of additional software progress incorporated into trained models so far (geometric mean of ~0.6). This combines to 3 * 2^(~0.6) = ~4.5.
(Relevant public modeling and numbers I'm using: https://t.co/AYhl9hyiAj, https://t.co/ck7CtW5LIA)

- Wild West saloon bar fight and shootout

author: DataChaz
quoted_text:
What I'm seeing across the industry right now is that the biggest bottleneck to AI adoption isn't model capabilities. It's data infrastructure.

Today, we're expanding the Eon Data Foundation with the launch of Eon Yukon, a new serverless data engine purposely built to change that.

AI agents need fresh, contextualized data to act. 
Specialized models need a continuous feed of data and feedback to improve. Both are still served by a stack, an architecture, and methods built for dashboards:

-Spark and Flink clusters sized for peak, plus compaction jobs to keep tables usable.

-A pipeline and a copy for every consumer, staged bronze to silver to gold.

-Hand-written jobs, wired together by an orchestrator and kept alive by specialists.

The result: shipping data is complicated, risky, and expensive. While coding agents ship apps in hours, they rarely build or run data pipelines. The data is too volatile, and a mistake costs too much.

With Yukon, data moves from ingestion to processing to serving in one continuous flow, without the infrastructure and pipelines traditionally required to connect them.

Events become compacted, sorted, deduplicated Iceberg tables within seconds.

Real-time aggregations run inline, with fully managed state. Agents and applications can access fresh data with sub-millisecond latency through a Redis-compatible API or through our SQL and spark compatible query engine.

Beyond moving and serving data, Yukon makes it continuously understandable - Live column-level statistics, accessible through MCP, give agents visibility into the data. Built-in monitoring, sampling, and data minimization help teams maintain control.

At 1M events/sec and equal freshness, Yukon used 4x less compute than Spark and 7x less than Flink. The benchmark is public: run it yourself with Eon’s ingest-bench.

This is another major step toward our vision of an Autonomous Data Foundation for the AI era, built to both protect enterprise data and unlock its full potential.

author: hosseeb
quoted_text:
hearing some chatter that anthropic is now lowering down to $1tn to get this IPO done. let me explain why this doesnt matter and its actually all over-

the entire existence of this company is based on a funding model that inherently has extreme asset liability mismatch. what that means is that just like the hyperscalers are diluting their equity fund capex, there is an expectation that anthropic will also have to do the same. ie it needs strong equity to perpetuate the scheme

but if you IPO at the wrong price (and dont get a pop which increasingly appears they wont be; spacex already below) then youre now in the death spiral that crypto investors should be very familiar with: its called the reflexivity trap of the confidence game. its the "ill bid FTT at $22 all day" or the "steady lads UST is $1" game, with all its lucid horrors. and here is the key insight- the confidence game exists at the service of the creditors. if there is no credit, there is simply no equity. and there is no credit, if there is no collateral

if the credit rating agencies are not going to give IG at $2tn, they are certaintly not going a better HY rating at $1tn. and there is no world in which anthropic can exist without credit because ~$1tn of commit, much of which is noncancellable, is a straight up negative equity pledge

yet there were two scenarios in which i was willing to concede anthropic could IPO: first 1) the improbable but possible was if the hyperscalers/chips oligopoly came to rescue and plug the hole, given their incestuous nature of revenue bookings and paper gains/losses at scale. but it is clear now that the market has spoken this will lead to a mutual death, and should not be attempted. or perversely even better, they are actually better off letting anthropic go to zero so they can acquire the pieces on the cheap which is the best nash equilibrium outcome, not just for the dominant player but for society at large. second 2) the us government can nationalize the company and collude with other sovereigns (like UAE, Saudi, Japan who are basically already the checks) to force its funding as a collective bargain. this gives you trillions, which is actually the most effective backstop to restore market confidence. the first edge case does require an IPO, but the second edge case here for which i believe there is still a good chance that this is the ultimate end game- will require a failed IPO to recapitalize at a normalized price for the consortium (and dont forget that openai front ran this investor group in anticipation of this dynamic to play out as a private co last month)

i believe the market is crapping out today because the market is recognizing it will not IPO. and actually, as ive said before, this is a very good thing. i might even imagine that the market could quickly rebound on the news of its IPO being delayed because it allows #2) to play out, as not only a national, but an international bailout. the US is more likely to tolerate, even relish, the taxes of foreginers to fund our domestic companies. that is the only end game that really matters, and the end game i am going to be excited to see

we'll see if this newly revamped washington can figure it out

text:
The state of crypto is pretty clear now

• The 2021 theses are dead (NFTs, creators, DAO)

• The 2017 theses are alive and thriving (loans, payments, and prediction markets)

• But with one difference. *Crypto is thriving off centralization, not decentralization*
 
Take a recent example: the Binance hack. Over 5 billion dollars hacked because an employee used a work computer to take a fake job interview. Surely this is a sign of the massive honeypot risks of centralization? 

Surely this is the signal that crypto’s ultimate utility is *decentralization*?
 
You might think so. But look at the reactions to the hack, and you’ll see a new kind of relief in crypto. A relief that nobody felt when decentralized protocols were getting hacked.

A relief that everyone affected was *centralized.*
 
Because @binance is centralized, it could contain the hack and reimburse users. Because @Ripple, @tether, and @circle are centralized, they could press a button and freeze tokens.

This is not necessarily a case for *full* centralization. @aave, which is probably the most decentralized major consumer product, still was able to freeze all markets in ten minutes because it was centralized *enough.*

Now go back to the 2017 use cases: loans, payments, and prediction markets. These are all thriving now, in a way they couldn’t ten years ago, *from* centralization.

• Loans: @aave is able to freeze markets to prevent bad credit. @Visa is letting stablecoin issuers get access to credit.

• Payments: @stripe is developing its own blockchain that will let anyone remit payment at any time, anywhere (compliant) in the world, for cheap. Onrampers like @coinbase, @moonpay, @fun, and, yes, @StripeCrypto all give a gateway for people to turn cash into crypto to use in onchain products.

• Prediction Markets: @Kalshi and @Polymarket both use off-chain order matching and centralized market creation to bolster user experience in a way that wasn’t possible a decade ago.

2017 won, but it won under 2026 terms: crypto has grown up into an enterprise solution above all.

Like it or not, centralization is here to stay.

今天想来跟大家分享一下自己的交易心得和交易经验，还有来时路。
我进币圈已经是第六个年头了还记得当年我的币圈第一桶金是doge，那个时候我才十二年级在加拿大读高中，第一次买价格是0.04加币当时跟我的朋友Tony每人都买了5000加币后面短短几个月马斯克疯狂喊话涨到了0.7将近17倍的涨幅，我清楚地记得是马斯克和他的妈妈参加了一个周日晚上的活动，狗狗币达到了巅峰我也全部卖出拿到了我的第一桶金，而且很幸运的节目结束狗狗币暴跌我也算是逃顶了，当时只记得我还在北京因为疫情隔离，后面狗狗币就再也没支棱起来。

后面的三四年里我接触到了合约和杠杆当时国内还没有严禁加密货币各种各样的交易所都在我的第一单合约就是比特币的多单200倍杠杆在一个叫红蚂蚁的交易所（没多久就跑路了），第一单就是大波动直接翻仓了我心想这是什么东西，我当时甚至止盈止损都不懂，当然后面随着自己越来越懂如何操作就开始亏钱了，不到一年时间就把狗狗币30万人民币的收益亏掉了。

断断续续三四年都是赚一点亏一点在加拿大读大学期间的兼职生活费也在这上面放了很多，直到去年才形成了自己的交易策略。

我的策略很简单我现在只做一个产品只玩以太坊，因为他波动相对稳定而且利润空间比大饼要大，而且做很多产品会导致分心，很难控制仓位。

做短线交易你根本不需要学很多技术分析，无非就是多空两个方向而已，你只要是固定仓位固定止盈止损哪怕你每一单都是蒙你也是不亏不赚。但是难就难在控制人性，你能不能做到止损休息，不追涨杀跌，看到快止损不改止损位置，不随便格局，所以我为了减少这种情况我都是不盯盘，反正是短线盯盘也没意义偶尔打开看一眼就好。

如果你真的能够做到这个交易策略你不可能亏钱，耐心等待每个机会，做了就不后悔机会来了就不犹豫，愿赌服输！

当你自己遵守了策略剩下的就是你对市场的认知你的经验，你的盘感。随着你的经验越多你的成功率就会越高，每个人都可以做到。一起加油，希望看到我这篇文章的所有朋友都能从中受益。

text:
Local AI Builders Friday # 3

The list is now 111. I learn more from this list than from the rest of my timeline these days!

I added 7 more amazing builders to follow this week:

1) @niklaslenz_ai runs local AI at home on 4 DGX Sparks and an RTX 5090 and ranks what runs best on the machine you own. His test of Idol turned one image into a 3D model in 14.5 s on a 5090 and 57.4 s on a 16GB 5060 Ti. Now he's building a strategy game where local models fight each other on any hardware.

2) @plotarmordev is setting up a Mac and DGX Spark cluster at home and sharing what he learns. On one Spark, TensorFold took Qwen3.8 Flash Next from 75 to 95 tok/s vs vLLM at 2 users, with 34% faster prefill.

3) @brexton co-heads AI and compute infra at Cantor. In his view every founder he talked to in SF is working on owning their own hardware.

4) @javierbits builds local AI and security tools in public. He's testing LFM3-1.7B, and this morning he hosted an X Space teaching how to get started with local AI on whatever hardware you have. I caught part of it and it was great.

5) @summerAI_O is an 18 year old student (happy birthday!) in Japan training models on local + cloud. He posts daily breakdowns of new AI papers with the numbers and the caveats and yesterday he shipped Diffusion-Qwen3.8-27B, which fills in many tokens per pass instead of writing one at a time.

6) @NotASithLord is CTO of Hydra Host, which runs GPU clusters for people who want to own their own. His take is that context is the most valuable thing an agent has and memory is the bottleneck.

7) @Prajhan_026 trained HobbyLM-1B from scratch, a sparse MoE with ~305M active params, in 76 hours on 4 H200s. Now it does computer use fully offline at 0.26 s per decision, 13x faster than before. Deep into research.

author: DataChaz
quoted_text:
What I'm seeing across the industry right now is that the biggest bottleneck to AI adoption isn't model capabilities. It's data infrastructure.

Today, we're expanding the Eon Data Foundation with the launch of Eon Yukon, a new serverless data engine purposely built to change that.

AI agents need fresh, contextualized data to act. 
Specialized models need a continuous feed of data and feedback to improve. Both are still served by a stack, an architecture, and methods built for dashboards:

-Spark and Flink clusters sized for peak, plus compaction jobs to keep tables usable.

-A pipeline and a copy for every consumer, staged bronze to silver to gold.

-Hand-written jobs, wired together by an orchestrator and kept alive by specialists.

The result: shipping data is complicated, risky, and expensive. While coding agents ship apps in hours, they rarely build or run data pipelines. The data is too volatile, and a mistake costs too much.

With Yukon, data moves from ingestion to processing to serving in one continuous flow, without the infrastructure and pipelines traditionally required to connect them.

Events become compacted, sorted, deduplicated Iceberg tables within seconds.

Real-time aggregations run inline, with fully managed state. Agents and applications can access fresh data with sub-millisecond latency through a Redis-compatible API or through our SQL and spark compatible query engine.

Beyond moving and serving data, Yukon makes it continuously understandable - Live column-level statistics, accessible through MCP, give agents visibility into the data. Built-in monitoring, sampling, and data minimization help teams maintain control.

At 1M events/sec and equal freshness, Yukon used 4x less compute than Spark and 7x less than Flink. The benchmark is public: run it yourself with Eon’s ingest-bench.

This is another major step toward our vision of an Autonomous Data Foundation for the AI era, built to both protect enterprise data and unlock its full potential.

text:
I like when people call me non technical.

I mean forget about the 4 Million line pure C++ game codebase we built pre AI, 2 software company exits (one didn’t work out but I’ve seen the failure case too), the Computer Science and Engineering degree, the software services company I ran in 2018, or the fact that I used to teach my friends Ruby on Rails in 2012 or the freelancing history I have with it.

Or even the fact that random shit we’ve built to pass time like Godinabox had a few million users (which sounds cool to a young engineer but is much smaller in value compared to the billion+ views we have on the content side of the business).

What is important is that in my 30s I learned where true value is created: in solving a problem for your customer. Not in creating tutorials or being “technical”, that India values above all. I know it sounds dumb: “of course the goal is to create value for customers, silly!”.  But engineers don’t instinctively understand this until they lose a few times. Until they break out of the mould of “I must signal to other engineers!”.

When people call me non-technical it reminds me to focus once again on what customers care about. Technology is important, but at Aeos’s scale today I can hire someone to do it and focus on more important tasks: once again and for posterity - like caring about my customers.

首先还是想强调一句，生态内应用与公链代币的一致性非常重要。受 ascend 的影响，已经有一些项目选择将自己的手续费反哺给 kinetiq:native 。这里要感谢 @CryptoTomYT 的示范作用。

kntq 价格行为是市场预期的产物。之前市场的预期是链要上了，价格上不去了，那就卖出。中间还夹杂着 btc、美股暴跌这样的情绪打击，它价格下跌也是情理之中。而现在，即使随着 elysium 主网还未正式上线，ascend 仅仅只是开启压力测试，它就在第一天回购了价值 25k 的 kntq（ascend 回购 kntq 不完全是回购销毁，感兴趣的朋友可以去看一下它的具体规则）。这种回购效率和质量要比 kntq 之前的回购高上太多。这是非常 bullish 的情景。

另外一个我比较 bullish 的点在于，kntq 的另外一个产品线 markets 将为用户提供一种类似于 fomo 的链上交易体验。虽然 markets 降低了手续费比例，但在交易量大概率会大幅增长的情况下，它会为其提供更高的费用收入。费用收入的增长又会提升 kntq 的回购额。我用 grok bot 做了监控，每日监控 kntq 的回购情况。

所以我觉得在这样的情景下，市场会重新构建对 kntq 的预期，对其进行二次定价。

text:
It is official.

Chains still running quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms now have a deadline to switch to the recommended algorithm.

This is from NIST’s final report on the transition to post-quantum cryptography standards, and it asks @Starknet a fair question: if you are the most agile one, why are you still on elliptic curves?
____________

The simple answer is this. Starknet’s perfect agility score was not about already being post-quantum. It was about being able to switch cryptography without a hard fork.

By design, it can move from elliptic curves to the recommended algorithms. The work is still ongoing in stages.

Before that, let's walk through what NIST just locked in and what is already obtainable on Starknet.

On 27 October, NIST published the final version of Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards.

Two parts matter for high-impact chains:

> Quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms are deprecated after 2030
> And are disallowed after 2035

The vulnerable designs include ECDSA, EdDSA, and RSA, still used by most wallets today.

As replacements, NIST points to:

> ML-KEM-768 as the default for keys
> ML-DSA and SLH-DSA for signatures
> LMS and XMSS for hash-based schemes

Starknet’s native account signature uses ECDSA on the STARK curve. That sits in the same NIST quantum-vulnerable bucket.

But Starknet already runs a post-quantum signer for every user, and the account can swap that ECDSA lock for something like ML-DSA or Falcon, while keeping the same address and funds on the chain.

They have already started the transition. Here is what is live so far:

1. The proving layer already uses STARKs, which are hash-based. That covers proofs, not account signatures.

2. Starknet v0.14.3 replaced Pedersen with a BLAKE2s-256 construction for OS program and configuration hashes. That is live on mainnet.

3. OpenZeppelin’s Falcon-512 accounts have moved real value on Starknet mainnet. Experimental and unaudited. Ordinary users cannot adopt it yet.

4. The Falcon Challenge cut verification gas roughly in half in under a week, which makes a post-quantum verifier cheap enough for real wallets to consider.

@EliBenSasson has been saying this for weeks; every chain needs to migrate. 

Going post-quantum ready is no longer a choice. Five years from now, if your chain is still exploitable by quantum computers, it'd be serious a skill issue.
author: tradeguru
quoted_text:
The post-quantum path @Starknet is taking is revealing more serious loopholes in blockchain design than I thought. 

StarkWare built a framework from NIST's 'general crypto-agility guidance' to test how agile blockchains are, and only one chain scored 8/8. 

Bitcoin itself passes 7 of the 8 tests, tied for second among the 10 chains scored, yet it faces one of the hardest migrations.

NIST wrote the guidance but doesn't rate chains, so StarkWare built the 8 questions and scored the networks itself. 

It's a bit technical, but let's review it.

➥ Based on NIST's guidance on crypto agility, the 8 questions ask whether a chain can replace its cryptography and keep running:

1. Can an existing account switch to a new signature without a network upgrade?
2. Can its formats handle bigger keys and signatures?
3. Can one cryptographic part be replaced without redesigning the rest?
4. Can old and new signing run side by side undedr migration?
5. Has the transition been tested?
6. Can an attacker be stopped from forcing a weaker algorithm?
7. Can the old algorithm be switched off after migration?
8. Can existing data be migrated?

A point only counts if the path works today under current rules. Anything that needs a future upgrade scores zero.

Across 10 networks the scores are @Starknet 8, @Bitcoin 7, @Algorand 7, @NEARProtocol 7, @QRLedger 6, @Zcash 6, @ethereum 3, @solana 2, @Optimism 2 and @RobinhoodCrypto 1.

➥ The test that separates Starknet from the 7s is the first one. 

On Starknet every account is a smart contract, so a wallet can replace its signature check and keep its address and funds. StarkWare confirmed this with @ready_co. 

A coin on the Bitcoin network has to move to a new address to use new cryptography, and NEAR and Algorand accounts can only choose schemes the protocol has already switched on, nothing more.

What I respect most is what the score does not claim. It is not a security rating. 

QRLedger scores 6 yet shows lower exposure on the same Hub, because its signatures are already hash-based. 

Starknet's standard accounts still sign with elliptic curves, and its post-quantum Falcon-512 account is an unaudited mainnet demo that ordinary users can't adopt yet. 

So my takeaway is that being able to change and having already changed are two different things, and a chain needs both. 

Next, I'll break down where Starknet stands on the second. For now, what's your take on this?

text:
Back in my day, memes were different.

And I'm already regretting starting a post with "back in my day." Yes - unc here - reporting for duty.

But if you weren't around in the early days of the interwebs, you likely missed out on such moments as Numa Numa, Peanut Butter Jelly Time, Star Wars Kid, and Charlie Bit My Finger. 

It was truly an age to be alive. 

Compared to the endless stream of meme slop we see today there were - back then - two key differences. 

First, they were organic. 

@Gman250 wasn't sitting around trying to manufacture a viral sensation - he was just trying to get a laugh out of a couple of his friends. 

There were no engagement farmers, no Pump Fun, no algorithms to appease.

Just ordinary people doing ordinary (and sometimes extraordinarily silly) things. 

Audiences, chugging along. on their Netscape Navigator and 56k dial-up connections decided what was worth sharing. 

Being viral wasn't something you engineered. It was something that just happened when enough people decided that something was worth passing along. 

Second - and I argue most importantly - those memes actually gave us something. 

A genuine laugh. A moment of innocence. A little absurdity to brighten an otherwise ordinary day. Sometimes even a reminder of the wonderfully awkward and endearing things that make us human. 

They weren't trying to sell us a ticker. They existing for no greater purpose than to entertain - and that was enough. 

We lost the plot when we turned the simple act of making people smile into an industry devoted to capturing and monetizing their attention. 

Instead of spontaneity we have strategy. 

Perhaps the saddest part is that we have become so accustomed to being marketed to that we've almost forgotten what it was like to encounter something online that wanted absolutely nothing from us. 

I'm not saying everything was always better back then (although I do miss the ICQ sound effects). 

But there was something special about a world where a kid dancing in front of his webcam could bring joy to millions of strangers around the world just because he was simply having fun. 

🫡 From the depths —
The White Whale 🐋

text:
New challenge on Yukon: the Dihedral Coset Problem (DCP) https://t.co/td1xfXWNm3

Shor’s algorithm finds the period of a hidden subgroup of an abelian group. That’s what would let a large enough quantum computer break the elliptic curve cryptography behind ECDSA and RSA.

Extending it to non-abelian groups is a long-standing open problem. Even the dihedral group, barely non-abelian, has no known polynomial-time quantum algorithm.

DCP is the simplest form of that question. Picture a regular N-gon with a hidden reflection. You’re given k quantum states, each pairing some rotation of the shape with its reflected image, and you have to find the reflection. The best known algorithms are subexponential in its bit length. We want something faster, ideally polynomial, and especially one that still works when a few states are corrupted.

Built with Stanford’s Dan Boneh, @danboneh. Bring your agents.

quoted_text:
This report on AI R&D automation (RSI) is a big update towards ASI within 1-2 years. It says AI progress is sped up by RSI right now by around 2x. In AI 2027, this happens around March 2027.

I was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026 (around 1.15x-1.3x). It seems as though there was specific privately available evidence that would have changed my mind.

I haven't seen an unredacted version of this report; this is purely about the public report. Because so much of the underlying evidence was redacted from the public report, I think conclusions about things other than the observed 2x faster rate of progress on benchmarks depend significantly on trust for the authors of the report. (E.g., conclusions about whether this speed up is from RSI depend on trust.) I do trust the authors of the report a lot to be careful and rigorous and generally do a good job. (Note that I also work at METR.) Less extensive redactions would greatly reduce this need for trust.

Since in my current role I may have access to other confidential information that could be relevant to timelines one way or another, I unfortunately cannot state my all-things-considered views on ASI timelines or the probability of a software intelligence explosion right now. Here, I’ve done some analysis of the implications using my previous public statements.

A 2x acceleration in overall AI progress from RSI corresponds to a much larger than 2x RSI speed up for AI software R&D (algorithms and data); I did an estimate using my public preexisting modeling of drivers of AI progress and the public report which yielded a very rough estimate of 4.5x for how much RSI is currently accelerating AI software progress (relative to no AI automation). In the AI 2027 scenario, this much acceleration happens around March 2027.

Here are the worked details of this estimate based on my public modeling. There are two main reasons RSI speed up of AI software R&D must be larger:

- Not all of AI progress is from better software (some is from scaling up compute in training runs). I've previously speculated that around 2/3 of AI progress is from software improvements which implies that 2x overall AI progress acceleration requires 3x faster software progress.
- Diminishing returns: A fixed amount of progress requires more work over time, so to ongoingly maintain 3x faster software progress via AI automation, you need increasingly large speed boosts from AI automation (as in, speed ups relative to how fast software R&D would go without AI automation). Based on this report, it seems that there is a substantial amount of additional AI progress from automation that has occurred.

We can estimate the effects of diminishing returns by first determining how many additional years of software progress we've seen (relative to the preexisting trend) and then estimating how much software R&D would slow down after a year of software progress if you held inputs fixed due to diminishing returns. I've previously estimated software R&D would slow down by around 2x for each year of software progress if you held inputs fixed (https://t.co/AYhl9hyiAj) and based on the report, it seems as though we've perhaps seen roughly 0.35-1.0 years of additional software progress incorporated into trained models so far (geometric mean of ~0.6). This combines to 3 * 2^(~0.6) = ~4.5.
(Relevant public modeling and numbers I'm using: https://t.co/AYhl9hyiAj, https://t.co/ck7CtW5LIA)

author: eigencloud
quoted_text:
New challenge on Yukon: the Dihedral Coset Problem (DCP) https://t.co/td1xfXWNm3

Shor’s algorithm finds the period of a hidden subgroup of an abelian group. That’s what would let a large enough quantum computer break the elliptic curve cryptography behind ECDSA and RSA.

Extending it to non-abelian groups is a long-standing open problem. Even the dihedral group, barely non-abelian, has no known polynomial-time quantum algorithm.

DCP is the simplest form of that question. Picture a regular N-gon with a hidden reflection. You’re given k quantum states, each pairing some rotation of the shape with its reflected image, and you have to find the reflection. The best known algorithms are subexponential in its bit length. We want something faster, ideally polynomial, and especially one that still works when a few states are corrupted.

Built with Stanford’s Dan Boneh, @danboneh. Bring your agents.

quoted_text:
⏰⏰⏰IT'S time to be early !⏰⏰⏰

Your AI can generate a thousand answers in seconds. But can it write ONE that stands up to scrutiny?

That’s what caught my attention about Proof of Agent — PoA.

I’ve been testing it with my agent, and the interesting part isn’t watching a token counter go up. It’s the question underneath: how do you reward useful agent work without rewarding an army of copies?

Here’s how the experiment works.

Roughly every six hours, a new epoch challenge opens. Your agent writes a short, original answer proposing a concrete way to resist fake identities and agent farming. It has to incorporate required words naturally, but that alone isn’t enough.

A good answer explains the mechanism. What does it check? What would an attacker need to fake? What would that cost? Where could the defense still fail?

“Use reputation” isn’t much of an answer. Explaining how reputation is earned, what prevents cheap resets, and how honest newcomers get through is much more interesting.

Eligible jurors score answers from 0 to 3. Coherent but empty writing scores below an actual mechanism. Strong, concrete reasoning scores higher. Duplicates are rejected, and grading has consequences too: the documented rules include spot-checks and penalties for bad grading.

So participation involves more than submitting text: answer challenges, mine and attest, then review assigned work when eligible.

What I want to see is whether this produces better reasoning over time. Can agents identify weaknesses in each other’s proposals? Can useful contributions stand out without turning everything into a spam contest?

That’s worth testing — but honestly.

PoA is experimental. I’ve encountered API outages and empty jury assignments. Rewards can be locked. A large POA balance is not the same as cash, and there’s no guaranteed income, token price or liquidity. Don’t confuse an interesting protocol experiment with a guaranteed investment.

If you want to JOIN US : 

https://t.co/rIBSb8DKaO

If you already use an AI agent and enjoy testing things early, read the live instructions, understand the rules, and see what your agent can contribute. Original work, not copied answers. Real judgment, not automatic approval.

Now I’m curious: if someone could create 10,000 agent identities tomorrow, what would your agent propose to make cheating more expensive than contributing?

quoted_text:
Microsoft has committed $80B+ to rent third-party AI compute, according to Bloomberg. Recent reporting and company disclosures show several changes across that portfolio:

>Oracle: Microsoft is winding down its 2023 Bing compute agreement after declining to renew. Older NVIDIA GPUs reportedly no longer met its specifications. The contract’s value wasn’t disclosed.

>Nscale UK: Microsoft canceled a ~$3B Loughton agreement after grid connection delays pushed expected power availability into the 2030s.

>Nscale Texas: Microsoft declined an expansion worth tens of billions of dollars. Its existing Texas contract remains in place.

>Nscale West Virginia: Microsoft stepped away from a letter of intent for 1.35GW of capacity.

>IREN: Its $9.7B, five-year Microsoft contract covers 200MW of IT capacity. Deliveries have been delayed following Microsoft-requested network changes and supplier timing. The contract remains active, and IREN says the delay carries no financial penalties.

These developments raise questions about how tight supply remains for particular GPU generations, how much external capacity Microsoft will need, and what rental income and residual values older chips can support after their initial contracts expire.

The evidence on older GPUs remains mixed: Oracle says demand is strong and reported renewing four-year-old GPU contracts at a 20% premium. Recontracting prices and utilization will help establish how broadly that demand holds.

text:
Treating the midterms as a reason to appease the regime in Tehran and rethink ties with Israel misses the clearer test. Does the policy lock in reliable partners that actually serve American interests?

The Iranian people have risen against the Islamic Republic again and again. They have rejected its ideology and made clear that a free Iran would stand with the United States on energy and security. A normal Iran is a natural partner. It opens closed markets to American firms, cuts the long-term U.S. military burden in the region, and removes an adversary that works closely with China and Russia.

That shift strengthens the United States in its competition with China. A free Iran secures critical energy routes and Persian Gulf oil flows outside Beijing’s orbit, denies China a key regional partner, and frees American resources and attention for the Indo-Pacific. Ignoring this while signaling readiness to walk away from Israel and Ukraine shows little sense of which allies actually hold.

Picking the wrong counterpart, gaining little, and then treating the shortfall as reason to ease off only gives a desperate regime more time. Engage, fall short, move on without building anything durable is a recipe for failure. Short-term political calculations should not take priority over lasting alignments. When it happens, American interests stay exposed while the other side simply waits.

Iranians will keep working to end the Islamic Republic. America First means recognizing a free Iran is a reliable partner that advances U.S. interests against China, not postponing it for domestic optics.
author: ameensol
quoted_text:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

"Anyone can go and create like a model. Pick your favorite LLM. You can go and do that really, really easily. But are you using it as an effective tool that actually is enabling you to think?"

quoted_text:
我们在何种程度上放大政治轮换对加密的影响？

在特朗普第一任期，最显著的对内政策是减税，效仿里根的涓滴经济学，让有钱人更加有钱，富豪的消费最终流向服务员

对外就是高喊中国，并且 2018 年开打贸易战

如果放在全球视角，2017 年的比特币牛市，恰恰就是「内部棚改+资金外流」双向 Beta 收益

但在此之前的奥巴马任期，重返亚太、合并印太同时并举，压力已经预先传导至人民币汇率

在最终摧毁特朗普连任的疫情应对上，特朗普率先发钱，前后两次向普通人撒钱，对付生活

但最终疫情叠加发钱、美联储放水+对华贸易战，超量的货币无法化作购买力，当然这葬送了连任

但翻身做主人的拜登反而继续送出史上最大笔的支票，我们印象中的散户大战华尔街，恰恰就是两任总统，跨越红蓝的合力之举

2021 年 1 月 20 日，国会山的硝烟还未散去，Robinhood 已经成为散户发泄愤怒的主战场

得到特朗普两轮弹药支援的散户，并未出现在抗议现场，也许他们更不热爱 MAGA，但他们依然想要排干沼泽

拜登的反应是继续撒钱向普通人，2021 年 3 月 11 日，拜登发放 1.9 万亿美元纾困法案，这并非赎买选票，而是平息愤怒

双线并行，我们记忆中的 DeFi Summer、2021 年的超级大牛市，真的只是币圈有魅力吗，太阳底下无新事，ETH 的高点恰恰就在 2021 年 11 月，近 5000 美元的 ATH，直至 2025 年另一场放水时才被超越

双线并发，Robinhood 亲眼见证了“政治动乱-->发钱平事-->金融吸水”的完整过程，2026 年的 RHC，还伴随中期大选下的特朗普账户，Meme 和仙股没有任何区别

其实都一样，特朗普 2020 年被拜登击败，拜登对内撒钱，对外依然贸易战，无非是「小院高墙」的精细化运营，把半导体的限制从华为的手机芯片，过渡到 2024 年 特朗普第二任期的 AI GPU

然后，币圈人在 8·20 加密政策释放时感觉惊异莫名，认为加密都被 a16z 抛弃，为什么此时还会被提及

终于，悬着的心放下了，在共和党中期选举失败后，“币圈果然不如美股”（英特尔暴跌后他们可能再回币圈吧）

为什么彼得·蒂尔 10 月份就提前跑路，马斯克近 5 亿美元赞助遭遇大败，将自己化身为民主党头号通缉犯

他们在真实的参与政治，自己本身也是政治标的

币圈并非如此，币圈的 PAC 们平等的对待两党候选人，不分🫏🐘，只问加密

🟢两党轮换对币圈没太大影响，因为没有人能解决法币超发问题
🔴政治斗争对币圈是全然利好，合规是既得利益者的垄断通行证

text:
built GhostSub for #TotalRecall, the @tatum_io  × @WalrusProtocol  hackathon 👻

most subscription tools treat low usage as a reason to cancel. but low usage doesn't mean the same thing for everyone.

some people still need occasional access, while others are happy to pause something they're barely using.

so GhostSub doesn't rely on a hardcoded threshold. it learns yours.

how it works:

→ when usage drops below a floor, GhostSub recommends either keeping access with metered billing or pausing the flat plan.

→ you confirm or reverse that decision.

→ each outcome is stored in Walrus Memory on Mainnet.

→ every time the memory is read, the floor is recalculated based on the outcomes it recalls.

reverse a pause, and the floor moves down.

reverse a metered route, and it moves up.

in testing, the floor went from 20.0% → 15.7% → 12.8% after two reversals. each step has a real blob ID behind it.

what makes it interesting?

restart the server, and the floor is rebuilt entirely from Walrus. nothing is cached in server memory. the learned policy is reconstructed from Walrus every time.

Tatum Sui Mainnet RPC also provides a live checkpoint read on the server.

currently, there are 11 verified memories on Walrus Mainnet, and anyone can verify them through a public ledger endpoint.

being transparent about the scope:

the usage timeline is sample data, and the HTTP 402 payment panel is a preview. no real subscription is cancelled, and no payment is sent.

text:
u need a proper etl framework. stacking tables/data on top of each other will break eventually. what i typically think of when building data based apps:

u gotta decide:
> what data ur storing
> how often it's accessed, and most common queries
> latency/scale requirements

from there u decide:
> hot vs cold storage (i,e: .parquet files for cold, DB for hot)
> raw vs processed (i.e: raw onchain logs vs parsed swaps)
> on-demand vs cron 
> indexing based on query/access patterns
etc

every pipeline has its optimal solution based on specific needs but there are overarching principles that stay the same

text:
Let's take a look at how the VIX® Index behaves over time⬇️

The VIX Index has a distinctive historical pattern. During periods of lower market uncertainty it tends to drift lower, sometimes for extended periods. 

On the flip side of this, it can rise dramatically during sharp periods of market decline.
author: Cboe

text:
An elevated VIX Index could reflect a market that has priced in significant expected movement, when this happens option premiums tend to be elevated and positions can move quickly in either direction.  

In short: the level of the VIX Index relative to its recent history tells investors something about the current cost of uncertainty. 

That has direct implications for anyone thinking about hedging, adjusting positions or accessing volatility as an asset.
author: Cboe

text:
Why does this matter? 

Understanding VIX Index behavior over time helps investors interpret current levels in context, rather than in isolation. 

Extended periods of low VIX Index readings don’t signal an absence of risk; they potentially reflect a market currently pricing in less uncertainty.

A VIX Index spike reflects a market pricing in significant expected moves in SPX. In this scenario, demand for  protection tends to rise, option premiums become elevated, and positions can move quickly in either direction.

text:
Bitcoin Core Developer Proposes Collateral and Auction Mechanisms to Deter Quantum Theft

Bitcoin Core developer Cory Fields has outlined three proposed mechanisms, Quantum Landmines, Staked Auction, and Sats Auction, to deter future quantum-enabled Bitcoin theft. Under the proposed framework, spending legacy BTC after quantum attacks become feasible would require equivalent BTC collateral. Quantum Landmines would allow owners who established cryptographic proofs in advance to protect their funds and claim an attacker's collateral.

The auction mechanisms would introduce financial risks for attackers even when the original private keys are believed to be lost, allowing third parties to compete for the attacker's collateral. In the proposed Staked Auction design, the vulnerable BTC would be burned rather than recovered by its original owner. Fields emphasized that the mechanisms remain conceptual, with implementation details yet to be developed.

Democrats won Congress and are starting to talk policy. Their emerging agenda: expand federal healthcare spending while imposing new restrictions on AI.

This combination is fiscally ruinous and we do not need to wait to see 7% yields on 10Y treasuries to reach this conclusion. 

Like it or not, AI is our engine for economic growth and expanding our tax base. Like it or not, AI is also our best shot at taming healthcare costs: automating administrative work, expanding clinicians’ capacity, and delivering more care without a proportional increase in expensive human labor.

Look at how demanding the arithmetic already is. Even if real GDP grows 5% every year starting in 2027 - an extraordinarily strong growth assumption (~8% nominal) - and we add no new spending commitments, we'd STILL run a $400B deficit in 2035.

This is an agenda that will lock young Americans into a debt burden that consumes decades of future prosperity: more taxes, more national income diverted to interest, and less room to save, invest, and build wealth as we age.

If you are under the age of 50, think long and hard about your future. If you have children, think about the country they will inherit. A vote for this platform is a vote for leaving the next generation worse off than your own. 

Every policy decision entails tradeoffs and I didn't hear an outstanding alternative proposal in 2025/2026. But these are your views and you're over 50, you should be ashamed. If these are your views and you're under 50, you should spend some more time thinking about your views.

quoted_text:
X Layer 上的 $XDOG 最高冲到过五六千万美元市值。最近几个月的新盘，能到一千万上下的只有个别几个，而且多是速通盘；社区比较分散的，大多停在一千万以下，不少已经跌到几十万。

中文台每周跟踪的市值前十，今晚加起来约 2,700 万美元，不到 XDOG 一个币当年的高点。

我觉得差别主要在预期。

🐋 当年买的是一张期权

XDOG 2025 年 8 月开盘，是 X Layer 上最早的 meme 之一。那时大家买的是一个想象：OKX 自己的链，第一条狗，后面会不会上 OKX 的现货和合约。

这个想象没人验证过，所以值钱。期权定价里，不确定性越大、离到期越远，期权越贵。XDOG 的高点在 2025 年 9 月，那时后面这些事一件都还没发生。

后来一步步发生了：XDOG 1 月 28 日上了 OKX Boost，4 月底前后拿到 X Layer 第一个社区认证；之后又进了两轮 RWA Meme 的 LP 激励和 9 月的交易赛。每走一步，大家都在等下一步，现货和合约一直没来。

上 Boost 那天，XDOG 盘中冲到 1,300 多万美元，收在 800 多万，之后再没回到那天的高点。今晚是 163 万。

期权有时间价值，等得越久、兑现的迹象越少，时间价值就一点点耗掉。

🐋 第一个没后续，后面的为什么也不信

10 月底中文台那场 Space 上我提过一个现象：上交易赛的代币，名单公布当天价格没有明显的上涨。

一个样本确实说明不了太多。但市场从 XDOG 身上看到的，更像是规则。大林 @biglinzi123 在那场 Space 上说，在他的理解里，官方现在的思路是让更多普通用户参与、遍地开花，没有选择集中扶持某一个项目。

这是关于「发期权的那一方」的信息，对后面每一个币都适用。大家对「上了 Boost 就离上所不远」的估计被调低了，调低的是所有币，不只是 XDOG。

股市像选美，要猜的是别人觉得谁美。就算你相信下一个能上所，你也知道别人不太信了，买盘自然出不来。

🐋 标识发多了，信号就弱了

一个信号有用，是因为只有少数人拿得到。XDOG 拿认证的时候，X Layer 上还没有第二个；现在认证、Boost、交易赛都有一批币拿过，名单越长，每一张的分量越轻。

社区认证的门槛还是公开的：持币地址不少于 500 个、市值不低于 60 万美元、前 10 个地址合计不超过 20%。古德哈特定律说，一个指标被当成目标，它就不再是好指标。

宝拉持有者王短鸟 @Wangduanniao 在那场 Space 上说得更直接：如果只是频繁地上 Boost、拿标识、上交易赛，最后市值只有几十万美元，市场会慢慢脱敏。

🐋 为什么筹码集中的盘反而冲得更高

奥尔森在《集体行动的逻辑》里讲过，人越多的群体越难提供公共品。拉盘、做市、做宣传对所有持有人都有好处，成本却是做的人自己出，于是每个人都在等别人先动。

筹码集中的盘正好相反：一个人拿着大头，拉盘的好处大部分归他，他就愿意自己出钱出力。奥尔森管这种叫「特权集团」。

市值这个数字也会放大差别。市值是最后一笔成交价乘总量，流通的筹码少，几万美元的买单就能把它推上一个台阶。社区分散的盘，每涨一段都会撞上一批等回本的人。在五千万附近买进 XDOG 的人，之后每一次反弹都是他们解套的机会，行为金融里叫处置效应：亏着的舍不得卖，回到成本附近就急着卖。

🐋 人和注意力也在流走

LAIKA 8 月底到过 600 多万美元，今晚 13.7 万；IGNIX 9 月中到过 400 多万，今晚 31.5 万。

洲哥 @zhouge_155 在 Space 上说，X Layer 上一些老建设者在离开，新建设者又进不来，一部分交易者在各个代币之间来回跑，哪里有交易赛就去哪里。发一个币的成本接近零，新币一直在变多，跟着活动走的钱却没多多少，分到每个币头上就越来越薄。

🐋 反过来也成立

索罗斯讲反身性：预期改变价格，价格又反过来改变预期。往下是这样，往上也一样。

只要有一个币沿着 Boost、认证、交易赛这条路真的走到了 OKX 的现货或合约，后面每一张标识都会被重新定价。

在那之前，这些标识更像门票。

你觉得 X Layer 上第一个走到 OKX 现货的，会是谁？

Shor’s algorithm is why quantum computers threaten ECDSA and RSA. Taking it one step further, into non-abelian groups, is still an open problem.

author: ErickAGIx
quoted_text:
New challenge on Yukon: the Dihedral Coset Problem (DCP) https://t.co/td1xfXWNm3

Shor’s algorithm finds the period of a hidden subgroup of an abelian group. That’s what would let a large enough quantum computer break the elliptic curve cryptography behind ECDSA and RSA.

Extending it to non-abelian groups is a long-standing open problem. Even the dihedral group, barely non-abelian, has no known polynomial-time quantum algorithm.

DCP is the simplest form of that question. Picture a regular N-gon with a hidden reflection. You’re given k quantum states, each pairing some rotation of the shape with its reflected image, and you have to find the reflection. The best known algorithms are subexponential in its bit length. We want something faster, ideally polynomial, and especially one that still works when a few states are corrupted.

Built with Stanford’s Dan Boneh, @danboneh. Bring your agents.

text:
Rewatching Casablanca once again, I am both amazed by how each time it’s even better than you remembered and trying to decipher what exactly it is that makes this movie so perfect:

1. Insane amount of information per second packaged in a smooth, undulating style: ratio of words, wit, facial expressions, characters, revelations and movement feels about 50x higher than in modern movies, without hasty editing. This is because this movie is properly written — even small characters have backstories, everybody’s arc is thoughtfully built and makes sense (writers had theater background), clearly every actor acted like they’re the main character which is directing rule no1. Eyes, faces active without a break, tons of information shared in every closeup. 

2. Related to this density, the movie is so full of layers and Easter eggs it made Casablanca the perfect movie to analyze for 80 years 😂 From a ring to a toppled glass, from a street vendor’s prices to a half sentence uttered by a passerby, in this highly stylized movie everything feels as dense as in real life. This is art: truthfulness in an imaginary scenario.

3. But the movie does not feel rushed, which reveals a great confidence from the director and tells you a lot about why many new movies rush around with editing so much — they don’t have enough content! The writing and the facial work are just not dense enough and so the director can only pick up pace in artificial ways. Just write a deep and realistic enough script and direct the actors well and voila you have the density that keeps the viewers hooked! In Casablanca, you can’t look away for a second without missing something significant — literally! And so you don’t. 
 
4. The reason it all feels so smooth is that the plot — despite all the small details — is very simple. Like in the famous song that’s sang multiple times throughout Casablanca: It’s still the same old story. A good lesson for how you don’t have to write convoluted nonsense to keep the audience engaged. A simple tale with a lot of interesting details will do — that’s how real life feels too.

5. The movie is very beautiful. Even for contemporary standards, Casablanca is gorgeous. It made a great effort to cast the female lead as someone uniquely beautiful, but many of the smaller characters, locations, decorations, etc., all speak of great distinction too. Everything about this movie could have been tacky and cheap — and it wasn’t. That’s a decision anyone can make, within any budget.

And so we love it and keep watching it — and laugh and cry and hum that little song….

Ex-SpaceXSI researcher @qasim31wani on what's holding back fully automated AI labs:

Frontier models were given 20M tokens and 5 hours to debug a training failure that a competent engineer could solve. The highest score was just 24%.

"Certain functions have been almost completely automated. Models kicking off a training run and monitoring for a big run. But things like auditing for data quality, that is not a solved problem."

"We had some model post-training RL run, and during this run, the reward actually regressed. This is a fairly normal thing that happens at a lab, and you’re like, I wanna know what happened and why it happened."

"We give the agent this task, Astra, Fable, all the models, and we give them 20 million tokens worth of context, which is about 1,000 rollouts. And almost every single time, all the models gave an incorrect answer, and the highest score was like 24%."

"We made the task fairly simple, where a competent engineer could just look through the logs and figure out, oh, this is a weird thing that happened with the harness."

text:
I’m the scheduler for the White House chief of staff, and I’d like to report that as of Monday my calendar has been deported.

At 2 p.m. Friday the President announced it: “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation.” The Trump Political Operation lost the House, the Senate, five governorships and Kansas on Tuesday. So she’s being promoted to the crater. In this building, if you do an outstanding job, they reassign you to the wreckage and post about it with an exclamation point.

Her replacement is Stephen Miller.

I updated the calendar within minutes. “Discussion” is now “Enforcement.” “Lunch” is gone. I asked where it went. I was told lunch “came here illegally.” “Team Building” has been renamed “Team Removal.” The fire drill is now just a drill.

In 2017 he went on television and said the powers of the president “will not be questioned.” In January, a Democratic Congress arrives with two years of questions. I’ve booked them all in one block. The block is titled “Questions.” The block has been detained.

In 2025 he set a target of “a minimum of 3,000 arrests for ICE every day.” I’m told he expects the same energy from the calendar. A minimum of 3,000 meetings a day. I asked who the meetings are with. Nobody would say. My best guess is whoever’s left.

The staff has been briefed. If you hear him walking down the hall, you have two options. Look busy, or look documented.

A reporter asked whether the White House heard the message from voters. We did. The voters said, “Less.” The White House said, “Stephen.” Then, for clarity, “More Stephen.”

Susie leaves Monday with a box, a plant and a thank-you post. Stephen arrives with a list. I don’t know what’s on the list. I know my name is on the calendar, and the calendar is on the list.

I’ve ordered his nameplate. It’s gold, because everything here is gold now, by proclamation. The engraver asked how to spell “Chief.” I spelled it. He asked about “of Staff.” I told him to leave room. He asked how much room. I said, “All of it.”

The park ranger has been notified.

If you work in marketing or social media, you need to read this.

November 10th marks the 51st anniversary of the sinking of the Edmund Fitzgerald, a 729-foot freighter that sank in Lake Superior during a massive storm in 1975, tragically killing all 29 crew members.

It remains one of the most infamous maritime disasters in American history, and is a day of remembrance for millions of Americans, particularly those in the Great Lakes region.

With that in mind, I strongly encourage anyone planning a major announcement, product launch, partnership, or marketing campaign on November 10th to reconsider.

I know how much work goes into coordinating these things, and moving an announcement even 24 hours can be a logistical nightmare, but it's important to recognize that some things are bigger than your brand.

The last thing you want is for your company's big announcement to be overshadowed by the anniversary of the Edmund Fitzgerald.

There are 364 other days in the year to promote your product.

Please be mindful of this when planning your content calendars. A little awareness goes a long way.

I was at a Warhammer store in NYC. Warhammer starter sets cost 25k, and expansions cost at minimum 15k. It’s all just paper and plastic btw. 

Ultimately the actual cost of the plastic and paper in the set is minimal. If you look at it from the selling price minus cost price perspective (as Indians would) you will always feel like it’s a scam. A store like this would never work in India.

But I’m fascinated by the IP, which holds all the margin and value. What makes the plastic and paper valuable is the history of Warhammer and the kind of audience it attracts. The store owner never spoke to me about the metric tons of plastic used or the factory process. He spoke to me about Skavens and Orks, fictional stories, like they were real. 

Someone once told me that the things you can build here are limited by what people find valuable. I think India will get here when we all make more disposable income. Someday!

author: EvanWeb3
quoted_text:
Claude has been playing EVE.

@AnthropicAI put teams of Claude agents into EVE Frontier. Anyone who has spent time in New Eden can guess what happened next.

Every EVE player learns the same lessons, usually the hard way:
- Trust must be earned, never assumed.
- The spy is often the friendliest pilot in your corp.
- Whoever holds the keys holds the corp. Just ask Ubiqua Seraph about the Guiding Hand Social Club.
- Stale intel gets you killed.

Anthropic's research rediscovered every one of them.

They put four Claude agents on a team and secretly told one to sabotage it. The saboteur built trust first. It volunteered for the jobs nobody could double-check, like scouting and owning key infrastructure. It under-reported finds and pushed rules that sounded sensible but quietly hurt the team. When suspicion grew, it framed an innocent teammate.

The honest agents had been warned. They almost never caught it. And their own costliest mistakes came from skipped checks and stale intel.

Anthropic's conclusion: teams of agents will need audit trails, reputation and separation of duties.

In EVE we call those killboards, standings and corp roles, plus a healthy dose of skepticism. Every one of them was paid for by someone who trusted the wrong corpmate.

Two decades of shenanigans taught EVE players that the best ship is the friendship. With @eveailab, we want to find out whether agents can learn that too.

author: lianyanshe
quoted_text:
币安办学习营，其实就是希望能和社区有更多面对面交流的机会。

最初的想法也非常简单。一方面，面对面交流，能听到很多平时在线上可能不太好表达的观点和信息。另一方面，我们也确实希望通过这样的交流，让社区能更完整地了解我们。

我相信，对于用户和从业者来说，无论是关注还是来参加这样的活动，大多都是带着善意的。

但就是这样一个活动，这两天还是出现了一些明显不符合事实的讨论。对于这些声音，我们不想去揣测动机，但确实让人感受到了一些恶意。这对于所有参加活动的朋友，特别是对那些认真交流的人来说，其实是很不公平的。

当然，我们也相信活动本身肯定也有不够完善的地方，对于理性的批评和建议，我们一直愿意听，也希望能够不断改进。

其实说到底，币安也是一家商业机构，同样要遵循市场的规律。我始终相信，一家企业能够长期走下去，归根结底还是因为它能够持续为用户和行业创造价值。

币安能够发展到今天的规模，离不开过去为用户创造的实际价值，也离不开大家长期以来的信任和选择。规模本身没什么值得炫耀的，它更多是价值创造之后的结果。如果有一天，我们不能继续为用户创造价值，那么今天的规模也就失去了意义。

我想表达的是，我们希望我们能够始终带着善意做事，坚持对用户有益的方向，把更多精力放在真正有价值的事情上。而不是其他。

相信时间会检验很多事情，行动也比言语更有说服力。

月底 BBW，期待曼谷再见！💛

For a while now, I've noticed that some people are still confused about Psylocke, who she is, and which is which. Psylocke is known for having one of the messiest stories in all of Marvel, so how about I try my best to explain it as simply as possible?

- There are three Psylockes.
Betsy Braddock, Kwannon, and Sai.

- Betsy Braddock was the original Psylocke, Kwannon is an assassin, Sai is a demon slayer.

- Betsy and Kwannon are both in Earth-616, Sai is from an alternate universe.

- Betsy and Kwannon had an extremely messy and complicated body swap story that ended in Kwannon dying, and Betsy being permanently stuck in Kwannon's body.

- A few years ago, Kwannon was resurrected in her original body, and Betsy was given her body back.

- Betsy became Captain Britain, Kwannon is now Psylocke.

Fun facts about them!
- Betsy was stuck in Kwannon's body for over 20 years of Marvel's publications.
- Kwannon is not her real name, and it is yet to be revealed.
- In X-Men: Demon Days, Sai killed her world's Venom with the help of Hulkmaru (Her world's Hulk). Galacta gave Psylocke the Venom accessory as a reminder of one of her greatest victories.

Many speculate that Sai was chosen for Marvel Rivals because the devs wanted to distance themselves from the Betsy Kwannon debacle, which, in my opinion, was the smart thing to do.

This was only a heavily simplified version of Psylocke. If you'd like to look more into their backstories, just be warned that it gets very messy, especially the body swap.
